title: Bid, ask and the spread
teaches: Read a quote: the bid, the ask, the last and the spread, what you pay right now, why a wide spread costs you, and how the size at each price limits your fill.

sources.title: Understanding an ETF's spreads and volumes (ETF.com article on Fidelity's Learning Center)

facts.quote: The term “bid” refers to the highest price a buyer will pay to buy a specified number of ETF shares at any given time.
facts.claim: The bid is the highest price a buyer will pay right now, for a stated number of shares.

facts.quote: The term “ask” refers to the lowest price at which a seller will sell the ETF shares.
facts.claim: The ask is the lowest price a seller will take.

facts.quote: The bid price will be lower than the ask price and the difference between two prices is called the spread.
facts.claim: The bid sits below the ask, and the gap between them (ask minus bid) is the spread.

facts.quote: If an investor buys 200 ETF shares at the ask price of $60 and sells them immediately at the bid price of $59.50, the investor would incur a loss of $100.
facts.claim: Buying at the ask and selling straight back at the bid loses the spread on every share.

facts.quote: ETFs that are more liquid and have higher trading volume typically have tighter or smaller spreads.
facts.claim: More liquid, higher-volume funds usually have tighter spreads.

facts.quote: The spread can be thought of as a hidden cost to investors since spreads reduce potential returns.
facts.claim: The spread is a hidden cost of trading that comes out of your return.

facts.quote: A market order generally will execute at or near the current bid (for a sell order) or ask (for a buy order) price.
facts.claim: A market buy fills at or near the ask; a market sell fills at or near the bid.

facts.quote: the last-traded price is not necessarily the price at which a market order will be executed.
facts.claim: The last trade is not the price your market order is promised.

facts.quote: Generally, a market order will be executed immediately. However, the price at which a market order will be executed is not guaranteed.
facts.claim: A market order fills right away, but its price is not guaranteed.

facts.quote: In addition, parts of a large market order may execute at different prices due to lack of liquidity at a price at the time of execution.
facts.claim: A big market order can fill at several prices when one price does not hold enough shares.

facts.quote: An investor places a market order to buy 1000 shares of XYZ stock at $3.00 per share. The order could have 500 shares execute at $3.00 per share and the other 500 shares execute at a higher price.
facts.claim: Part of a market order can fill at the quoted price and the rest at higher prices.

facts.quote: A limit order is not guaranteed to execute.
facts.claim: A limit order may never fill.

facts.quote: The stop price is not the guaranteed execution price for a stop order. The stop price is a trigger that causes the stop order to become a market order.
facts.claim: A stop price is a trigger: once hit, the stop becomes a market order with no promised price.

facts.quote: While limit orders do not guarantee execution, they do help ensure that an investor does not pay more than a pre-determined price for a stock.
facts.claim: A limit order caps what you pay, at the cost of maybe not filling.

facts.quote: The reduced level of trading interest in extended-hours trading generally results in wider spreads between the bid and ask prices for a stock or no quotes at all.
facts.claim: Before and after the regular session, spreads are usually wider, or there may be no quote at all.

facts.quote: As a result, investors may find it more difficult to get their orders executed or to get as favorable a price as they could have during regular trading hours.
facts.claim: Wider extended-hours spreads make fills harder and prices worse than in the regular session.

facts.quote: Liquidity refers to the existence of buyers and sellers who are willing to trade with incoming orders and the degree of price competition among buyers and sellers.
facts.claim: Liquidity means there are buyers and sellers ready to trade with your order, competing on price.

facts.quote: “Price improvement” is the opportunity, but not the guarantee, for an order to be executed at a better price than the current quote.
facts.claim: You can be filled better than the quote (price improvement), but nothing promises it.

facts.quote: This type of order provides the most certainty that your order will be executed because it's not tied to any restrictions.
facts.claim: A market order is the surest way to get filled.

facts.quote: On the downside, you might not get the price you saw or were originally quoted, especially in fast-moving markets.
facts.claim: In a fast market, a market order can fill away from the quote you saw.

facts.quote: However, there's a chance your order doesn't get executed at all. For example, if the market price fails to match or better your limit price while your order remains active, it will not be executed.
facts.claim: If the market never reaches your limit price, your limit order does not fill.

facts.quote: The exchange-traded fund's median bid-ask spread, expressed as a percentage rounded to the nearest hundredth, computed by:
facts.claim: The SEC's ETF rule states the spread as a percentage, to two decimals.

facts.quote: Dividing the difference between each such bid and offer by the midpoint of the national best bid and national best offer
facts.claim: The SEC's ETF rule gets the spread percent by dividing ask minus bid by the midpoint.

facts.quote: For example, let’s imagine JKL stock is trading with the bid at $49.90 and the offer at $50.10. The spread is therefore $0.20.
facts.claim: Example quote: bid $49.90, ask (offer) $50.10, spread $0.20.

facts.quote: But if you wanted to buy JKL right now, you would probably have to pay $50.10. If you wanted to sell right now, all you’d get is $49.90.
facts.claim: Buying right now costs the ask; selling right now gets the bid.

facts.quote: The wider the spread, the more it will cost you to trade JKL.
facts.claim: A wider spread costs you more to trade.

facts.quote: Note, however, that spreads could be tight on both, which could mislead unwitting investors to conclude that both securities are equally liquid.
facts.claim: A heavily traded stock and a barely traded one can both show tight spreads, so the spread alone can mislead you about liquidity.

facts.quote: Typically, the number of shares offered on the bid or the ask will be small
facts.claim: The number of shares showing at the best bid or ask is usually small.

facts.quote: someone might be willing to sell you 100 shares of JKL at $50.10, but if you want to buy 10,000 shares, you might have to pay $50.25 or more.
facts.claim: The size at the ask covers only so many shares; a much bigger order pays higher prices.

facts.quote: The amount that you drive up the price of something you are trying to buy is called the market impact.
facts.claim: How far your own buying pushes the price up is called market impact.

facts.quote: If someone asked you what a share of JKL was “worth,” you would probably choose the midpoint, $50.00, or maybe the last price at which you can see a trade actually happened.
facts.claim: The midpoint and the last trade are reference values for what a share is worth, not prices you can trade at right now.

facts.quote: Limit orders are a particularly valuable tool for trading thinly traded securities, where even small orders have the potential to represent a high percentage of an ETF's average daily volume and, as a result, impact the prevailing market price.
facts.claim: In thinly traded names, limit orders help because even small orders can move the price.

facts.quote: By contrast, with a market order, you get the prevailing market bid or ask price.
facts.claim: A market order takes the bid (selling) or the ask (buying).

facts.quote: In general, smaller spreads are better, but context is key.
facts.claim: Smaller spreads are generally better, judged in context.

facts.quote: for example, 300 in the bid size column means that there are 300 shares or contracts ready to be bought at the respective bid price at the respective exchange.
facts.claim: Bid size is the number of shares buyers want at that bid price.

facts.quote: the bid area of the gadget is sorted in descending order by the bid price column, so that highest prices are on top. The ask side is sorted vice versa: the default sorting displays lowest prices on top.
facts.claim: On a Level II book, the best prices sit on top: the highest bid and the lowest ask.

facts.quote: Price improvement occurs when an order is executed at a price lower than the quoted offer when purchasing or a price higher than the quoted bid when selling.
facts.claim: Price improvement is a buy filled below the ask or a sell filled above the bid.

facts.quote: With respect to extended-hours trading, many brokerage firms currently accept only limit orders
facts.claim: In extended hours, many brokers accept only limit orders.

facts.quote: E58. No new buys outside regular trading hours.
facts.claim: Our rule: no new buys outside regular trading hours.

facts.quote: Answer the way a working trader says it: a market buy fills at the ask
facts.claim: The owner teaches it the trader's way: a market buy fills at the ask.

facts.quote: bid = the most a buyer pays right now, ask = the least a seller takes
facts.claim: Plain definitions: the bid is the most a buyer pays right now, the ask is the least a seller takes.
Worked steps for the spread percent: spread 0.10, midpoint 20.00, 0.10 divided by 20.00 is 0.5%.

facts.quote: Order-flow questions name the tool.
facts.claim: A question about shares at a price names the tool: Level 2 or time and sales.

walkthroughs.title: Two prices, one gap
steps: Every quote has two prices. The bid is the most a buyer will pay right now.
The ask is the least a seller will take. It sits above the bid.
The gap between them is the spread. Buy at the ask, sell at the bid, and that gap is your cost.

walkthroughs.title: What you pay right now
steps: Buy at market and you pay about the ask. Sell at market and you get about the bid.
Bid $49.90, ask $50.10. Buy now and you'd pay about $50.10. Sell now and you'd get about $49.90.
The last price is a trade that already happened. It is not a promise of your fill.

walkthroughs.title: Size: how many shares sit at each price
steps: Every bid and ask comes with a size: the shares waiting at that price.
On the full order book (Level II), the best prices usually sit on top: the highest bid, the lowest ask.
Size at the best price is often small. A bigger order reaches into worse prices.
Say 100 shares are offered at $50.10. Buy 10,000 and you might pay $50.25 or more.

questions.q: On a stock quote, what is the bid?
choices: The most a buyer will pay right now
The least a seller will take right now
The price of the last trade
The price halfway between bid and ask
questions.answer: The most a buyer will pay right now
questions.why: The most a buyer will pay right now. That is the bid, and it is what you get when you sell at market. The ask is the least a seller will take, and it sits above the bid. The last trade already happened. The midpoint is only a reference for value.
questions.lesson_line: The bid is the buyer's side of the quote.

wrong.The price of the last trade: That's the last price. It already happened, and the quote may have moved since.
wrong.The least a seller will take right now: That's the ask, the seller's side of the quote. It sits above the bid.
wrong.The price halfway between bid and ask: That's the midpoint. It's a reference, not anyone's order.

questions.simple: The bid is the highest price a buyer is offering right now, the buyer's side of the quote.

reasons: fixed before (distractor replaced by the checker)

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The ___ is the lowest price a seller will take right now.
questions.why: Ask. The ask is the lowest price a seller will take right now. It sits above the bid, the most a buyer will pay. The last is a trade that already happened, and the spread is the gap between bid and ask.
questions.lesson_line: Buyers bid, sellers ask. The ask is the seller's side of the quote.
questions.simple: The ask is the lowest price a seller will take, and it sits above the bid.

reasons: stable definition, Tier 1 sources

questions.q: On a stock quote, the bid is lower than the ask.
questions.why: True. The bid is the most a buyer will pay and the ask is the least a seller will take. The bid sits below the ask, and the gap between them is the spread.
questions.lesson_line: Bid below, ask above, spread in between.
questions.simple: True, the bid sits below the ask, and the gap between them is the spread.

reasons: the key rests on one quote (f3)

questions.q: On a stock quote, what is the spread?
questions.why: The ask minus the bid. The spread is the gap between the lowest price a seller will take and the highest price a buyer will pay. It is a hidden cost of trading right now. It is not the day's range, the day's change, or the midpoint halfway between bid and ask.
questions.lesson_line: Spread is ask minus bid. Read it before you place the order.

wrong.The day's high minus low: That's the day's range, how far price traveled today. It isn't a cost to trade.
wrong.Today's price change: That's the day's change. It says nothing about what it costs to trade right now.
wrong.The bid and ask averaged: That's the midpoint, a reference for what a share is worth. The spread is the gap, not the middle.

questions.simple: The spread is the ask minus the bid, the gap between what sellers want and what buyers offer.

reasons: the key rests on one quote (f3)

questions.q: A market buy fills at the last price you saw on your screen.
questions.why: False. The last price is a trade that already happened. A market buy almost always fills at the ask, the least a seller will take right now. The ask can sit above the last. In a fast market it can move before you fill.
questions.lesson_line: Last is history. A market buy pays the ask.
questions.simple: False, the last price already happened, and a market buy almost always fills at the ask.

reasons: stable rule, two Tier 1 sources

questions.q: You place a market order to buy. Near which price should you expect to fill?
questions.why: Near the ask. A market buy takes the sellers' price, so it fills at or near the ask. You get speed, not a set price: the price is not guaranteed. The last trade and the midpoint are not prices you can count on.
questions.lesson_line: A market buy pays at or near the ask. That's the price of getting in right now.

wrong.Near the bid: That's roughly what you'd get selling. A market buy doesn't wait for a seller to come down.
wrong.At the last trade: The last trade already happened. Your fill comes from the quote as it stands now.
wrong.At the midpoint: The midpoint is a reference. You might get a better fill, but expect the ask.

questions.simple: A market buy pays about the ask, because that is the lowest price a seller will take right now.

reasons: stable rule, Tier 1 and Tier 2 sources agree

questions.q: The spread is a cost of trading, even when the commission is zero.
questions.why: True. The SEC calls the spread a hidden cost, because it cuts into your return. Buy at the ask and sell at the bid, and you give up the gap on every share. A zero commission removes the fee, not the spread. The wider the spread, the more a trade costs.
questions.lesson_line: No commission doesn't mean free. Crossing the spread costs you.
questions.simple: True, buying at the ask and selling at the bid gives up the gap, even with no commission.

reasons: stable, Tier 1 and Tier 2 sources agree

questions.q: Bid $24.98, ask $25.02. What is the spread in dollars?
questions.why: $0.04. The bid is the most a buyer pays right now, $24.98. The ask is the least a seller takes, $25.02. The spread is ask minus bid: 25.02 minus 24.98 = 0.04. Buy at the ask and sell back at the bid, and you lose that 4 cents a share.
questions.lesson_line: Spread equals ask minus bid. Work it out before every order.
questions.simple: The spread is $0.04, because the ask of $25.02 minus the bid of $24.98 leaves four cents.

reasons: the key rests on one quote (f3)
computed key

questions.q: Bid $19.95, ask $20.05. What is the spread as a percent of the midpoint?
questions.why: 0.5%. The gap is $20.05 minus $19.95. Divide it by the midpoint, the price halfway between bid and ask, and write the result as a percent. The SEC's ETF rule measures spreads this way, rounded to the nearest hundredth. A percent lets you compare a cheap stock with a pricey one.
questions.lesson_line: Percent lets you compare spreads on cheap stocks and pricey ones.
questions.simple: It is 0.5%, the gap between bid and ask divided by the price halfway between them.

reasons: computed key
sources differ on the divisor (midpoint vs ask); the question names the midpoint, see conflicts

questions.q: Bid $9.80, ask $10.20. You buy 500 shares at the ask and sell right away at the bid. What did the spread cost you?
questions.why: $200. You paid the $10.20 ask and sold at the $9.80 bid. You gave up the full spread on each of the 500 shares. The SEC's own example works the same way: 200 shares bought at $60 and sold at $59.50 lose $100. A quick round trip at an unchanged quote costs the spread.
questions.lesson_line: Buy at the ask, sell at the bid, and you pay the spread. Wide spreads make quick exits expensive.
questions.simple: You lose $200, because you paid the ask and sold at the bid on all 500 shares.

reasons: the key rests on one quote (f4)
computed key

questions.story: You own a stock with a sell stop at $42.00. It trades down and the stop triggers. The quote now reads $41.90 bid, $42.05 ask.
questions.q: Near which price should you expect your shares to sell?
questions.why: Near $41.90. The stop price is only a trigger. Once it is hit, the stop becomes a market order. A market sell fills at or near the bid, the most a buyer pays right now. The price is not guaranteed: in a fast market the fill can come in below it. It is never a promise of $42.00.
questions.lesson_line: Your stop is a trigger, not a price. Expect the bid, or worse in a fast market.

wrong.Near $42.05: That's the ask, the price a buyer pays. You are selling, so you get the bid.
wrong.Exactly $42.00: The stop price only triggers the order. It is not a guaranteed fill price.
wrong.$42.00 or more: That treats the stop as a floor. Once it triggers it's a market sell, and the bid is already below $42.00.

questions.simple: Expect about $41.90, because a triggered stop becomes a market sell, and a market sell fills near the bid.

reasons: stable rule, Tier 1 sources

questions.story: On Level 2, the ask is $12.40 with 300 shares showing. More sellers wait at $12.45 and $12.50. You send a market buy for 1,000 shares.
questions.q: What should you expect from the fill?
questions.why: Some at $12.40, rest higher. The ask is the least a seller will take, and only 300 shares sit there. A market order fills right away against what is there. Expect the rest to fill against the sellers above it, at $12.45, $12.50 or higher. The SEC's own example works the same way: 500 of 1,000 shares fill at the quote, the rest higher.
questions.lesson_line: Read the size before you send size. A market order takes what's there, then reaches higher.

wrong.It waits until $12.40 has size: A market order doesn't wait for more sellers at your price. It generally executes right away, against the sellers who are there.
wrong.All 1,000 shares at $12.40: Only 300 shares show there. You can't count on more at that price, so expect the rest higher.
wrong.Some at $12.40, rest cancelled: A market order doesn't drop the rest. In the SEC's example, the other 500 shares could execute at a higher price.

questions.simple: Only 300 shares sit at $12.40, so expect some to fill there and the rest at the higher prices above it.

deeper.trap: The size on screen is a snapshot. By the time a big market order lands, those 300 shares may be gone and the next sellers may sit higher. FINRA warns you might not get the price you saw, especially in a fast market. A market order buys speed, not price.

reasons: fixed before (absolute wording softened by the checker)

questions.q: Your market buy for 1,000 shares fills 400 at $30.10 and 600 at $30.15. What is your average price?
questions.why: $30.13. Multiply each fill's shares by its price, add them up, and divide by the 1,000 shares. More shares filled at $30.15 than at $30.10, so the average sits closer to $30.15. That average, not the ask you first saw, is your real cost.
questions.lesson_line: When your order fills at several prices, your real cost is the average, not the ask you saw.
questions.simple: Your average is $30.13, because more of the shares, 600 of 1,000, filled at the higher price.

reasons: the key rests on one quote (f11)
computed key

questions.q: Fill the blank with the right word.
questions.sentence: The number of shares waiting at a quoted price is its ___.
questions.why: Size. The size is the number of shares waiting at a quoted price. A bid size of 300 means 300 shares wanted at that bid price. Price tells you where buyers and sellers stand; size tells you how many shares are there. At the best bid or ask, the size is often small.
questions.lesson_line: Price tells you where. Size tells you how many.
questions.simple: The size is how many shares wait at that price, like 300 shares wanted at the bid.

reasons: fixed before (moved from rung 4 to rung 3)

questions.q: A buy limit order at the bid will fill as long as the stock keeps trading.
questions.why: False. A limit order fills only if the market reaches your price. FINRA says that if the market price fails to match or better your limit, it will not be executed. Buy at the bid and the stock can trade up and away, leaving you unfilled. You get price control, not a promise of a fill.
questions.lesson_line: A limit order protects your price and gives up the promise of a fill.
questions.simple: False, if the price moves up and away, your limit at the bid just sits there and may never fill.

reasons: fixed before (statement reworded by the checker)

questions.story: You want to buy 2,000 shares. Level 2 shows four stocks. Each line reads bid / ask, then the shares at the bid / at the ask.
questions.q: On Level 2, which quote can you buy 2,000 shares into cleanly?
questions.why: 50.00 / 50.02 with 3,000 / 2,500. On Level 2, the ask side shows 2,500 shares at 50.02, enough for your 2,000. The spread is only two cents. The 49.70 / 50.30 quote has the size but costs sixty cents to cross. The 50.01 / 50.02 quote is tight, but only 100 shares sit at the ask, so the rest fills higher. Time and sales, the live list of trades, shows whether size really trades there.
questions.lesson_line: I want a tight spread AND real size at the price. One without the other costs you.

wrong.49.70 / 50.30 with 2,000 / 2,500: The size is there, but the spread is wide. You're well under water the moment you buy.
wrong.50.01 / 50.02 with 100 / 100: Tight, but only 100 shares at the ask. The rest of your order likely fills at higher prices.
wrong.49.95 / 50.05 with 1,500 / 1,800: Wider than the best quote, and 1,800 shares at the ask won't cover your 2,000. The rest likely fills higher.

questions.simple: Pick the tight quote with 2,500 shares at the ask, because it is cheap to cross and covers your 2,000 shares.

deeper.trap: The tightest spread on the board, 50.01 / 50.02, is the trap. Only 100 shares sit at the ask. Send 2,000 at market and the rest reaches into higher sellers. Your average can end up worse than a wider quote with real size. Read spread and size together, never one alone.

reasons: fixed before (story clarified by the checker)

questions.story: Stock A quotes $4.95 bid, $5.05 ask. Stock B quotes $199.90 bid, $200.10 ask. B's spread is wider in cents. You'd put the same dollars in either.
questions.q: As a percent of the midpoint, which spread costs more?
questions.why: A, by about 20 times. The midpoint is the price halfway between bid and ask. A: spread 0.10, midpoint 5.00, so 0.10 / 5.00 = 2%. B: spread is twenty cents, midpoint 200.00, so about a tenth of a percent. B's spread is bigger in cents, but its price is far bigger still. A's spread eats a big slice of a small price. With the same dollars in either, A costs far more to cross.
questions.lesson_line: Compare spreads in percent, not cents. A small spread on a cheap stock can cost the most.

wrong.B costs about 2x more: That's comparing cents. B's spread is bigger in cents, but its price is far bigger still.
wrong.They cost about the same: Same dollars in, very different cost. Work each spread out as a percent of its midpoint.
wrong.Can't tell without the size: Size matters for a big order, but this asks the spread as a percent of its midpoint. The two quotes give you all you need.

questions.simple: A costs more, about 20 times, because its small spread sits on a small price, so it eats more of each dollar.

deeper.trap: The cents trap. B's spread looks worse because it is more cents. But you pay the spread on every share, and the same dollars buy far more shares of the cheap stock. So the cheap stock's spread is paid many more times over. Compare spreads as a percent of price, never in cents.

reasons: computed key
sources differ on the divisor; 'about 20x' holds either way, see conflicts

questions.story: A stock reports earnings after the close. It jumps in after-hours trading. You pull up its quote.
questions.q: Compared with the regular session, what should you expect from the quote?
choices: A wider spread than in the day
A tighter spread, with all the news
The same spread as in the day
Fills right at the quote you see
questions.answer: A wider spread than in the day
questions.why: A wider spread than in the day. Fewer traders work after hours, so the gap between bid and ask is usually wider, or there is no quote at all. Orders can be harder to fill, at worse prices than in regular hours. Our own rule adds one more: no new buys outside regular trading hours.
questions.lesson_line: After hours, spreads widen and fills get harder. Our rule: no new buys outside regular hours.

wrong.A tighter spread, with all the news: News can feel like it brings buyers. But the SEC says lower trading interest after hours generally means wider spreads.
wrong.The same spread as in the day: The SEC says less trading interest after hours generally means wider spreads. Expect the quote to be wider than in the day.
wrong.Fills right at the quote you see: The SEC says after-hours orders can be harder to fill, at worse prices. The quote you see is not a promise.

questions.simple: Fewer people trade after hours, so expect a wider spread, and our rule is no new buys then.

deeper.trap: The news makes the stock feel busy, so the quote feels solid. But fewer traders work the after-hours session. The spread runs wider, and the price you see may not be one you get.

reasons: touches the owner's rulebook (E58 no new buys outside regular hours, taught in the why)
question text changed in wave6 (lineage entry needed)
broker practice in extended hours can change (f38 says 'currently')

questions.q: When a market buy fills below the quoted ask, that is price improvement.
questions.why: True. A buy filled below the quoted offer is price improvement: a fill better than the quote. The SEC calls it an opportunity, not a guarantee. Plan your trade on the ask, and treat a better fill as a bonus.
questions.lesson_line: Hope for price improvement. Plan for the ask.
questions.simple: True, a buy filled below the ask is called price improvement, but nobody promises it.

deeper.counter: The flip side: a market buy can also fill above the ask you saw. That happens when the quote moves fast or the size at the ask runs out. Both happen. Only the better fill is a bonus, so plan for the ask or worse.

reasons: stable, Tier 1 and Tier 2 sources agree

questions.q: Two stocks show the same tight spread. That means they are about equally liquid.
questions.why: False. Fidelity warns that a heavily traded stock and a barely traded one can both show tight spreads. That can mislead you into thinking they are equally liquid. The spread only shows the best prices. Liquidity means buyers and sellers ready to trade with your order. Check how much each stock trades, not just the spread.
questions.lesson_line: Same tight spread, different stocks. Check how much each one trades before you call it liquid.
questions.simple: False, a barely traded stock can show the same tight spread as a busy one, so check how much it trades too.

deeper.example: Picture two stocks, both quoted with the same tight spread. One trades heavily every day. The other barely trades. On the screen they look the same. Send a big market order into the thin one and it can fill at price after price. The spread was tight, but the market behind it was not deep.

reasons: stable, Tier 1 and Tier 2 sources agree

questions.q: You buy at the $20.30 ask. The bid is $20.00. Your stop is $0.40 under your fill. What percent of that $0.40 is the spread?
questions.why: 75%. The spread is $20.30 minus $20.00. Divide it by the $0.40 stop distance. Sell right after you buy and you would get about the bid. That is already most of the way to your stop, before the stock moves. I'd skip a name this wide.
questions.lesson_line: If the spread eats most of your stop room, the trade is broken before it starts.
questions.simple: The spread is 75% of your stop room, so you start most of the way to your stop.

deeper.trap: On the chart the stop sits $0.40 below your fill. But your real exit is the bid, and it already sits most of that distance below what you paid. One small dip and the stop fills. The wider the spread, the less room your stop really has.

reasons: computed key

questions.q: Once the price hits your stop, what happens to a stop order?
choices: It fills at exactly the stop
It only sends you an alert
questions.why: It becomes a market order. The SEC says the stop price is a trigger, not a guaranteed fill price. Once it is hit, the stop order becomes a market order. A market order generally executes right away, but its price is not guaranteed.
questions.simple: The stop price is only a trigger: once it is hit, the stop becomes a market order with no set price.
questions.lesson_line: A stop price is a trigger, not a promise. Once hit, you get a market order.

wrong.It becomes a limit order: The SEC says a triggered stop becomes a market order, not a limit order. Nothing sets the price you get.
wrong.It fills at exactly the stop: The stop price is not a guaranteed fill price. It only triggers the order.
wrong.It only sends you an alert: That's a price alert. A stop order acts on its own: once triggered, it becomes a market order that generally executes right away.

reasons: stable rule, Tier 1 source (SEC Understanding Order Types)

questions.q: Bid $19.95, ask $20.05. What is the spread as a percent of the midpoint, the price halfway between them?
questions.why: 0.5%. First, the spread is 20.05 minus 19.95, which is 0.10. Next, the midpoint, halfway between bid and ask, is 20.00. Then 0.10 / 20.00 = 0.005, which is 0.5%. A percent lets you compare a cheap stock with a pricey one.
questions.lesson_line: Spread divided by midpoint, as a percent. Percent compares cheap and pricey stocks.

wrong.0.1%: That calls the ten cent spread 0.1%. A percent needs the spread divided by the price: 0.10 / 20.00.
wrong.0.005%: That is the decimal 0.005, not yet turned into a percent. As a percent it is 0.5%.
wrong.5%: The decimal point slipped two places. 0.10 / 20.00 is 0.005, which is 0.5%.

questions.simple: It is 0.5%, the gap between bid and ask divided by the price halfway between them.

conflicts: Spread as a percent: SEC Rule 6c-11 (ETF disclosure) divides ask minus bid by the midpoint. Some references divide by the ask instead (I could not confirm Investopedia's wording: the site refused both the plain client and WebFetch). Every percent question names the midpoint. q09's prices give 0.50% either way; q17's 'about 20x' holds either way (20.0 by midpoint, 19.8 by ask).

Quote size units: Schwab's 'Round Lots Regulatory Changes' page (https://www.schwab.com/learn/story/round-lots-regulatory-changes, Oct 28, 2025) says brokers historically showed bid/ask/last sizes in round lots, and that from Nov 3, 2025 Schwab shows actual shares rounded down to the stock's round lot. Platforms differ, so no question asks what a size number means in units; every size in a question is a whole share count.

Minimum tick: the SEC's 2024 Regulation NMS amendments add a half-penny quoting increment for some stocks. Fidelity's ETF tips page says spreads 'can be as thin as $0.01'. Neither is used: no question states a minimum possible spread.

Fidelity's 'Understanding an ETF's spreads and volumes' is an ETF.com article hosted on Fidelity's Learning Center. It is filed under the publisher 'Fidelity Investments', the same as Fidelity Viewpoints, so the two can never count as two publishers under the support rule.
